contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you found external structures. Today: look inside an organism at its internal structures!

An internal structure is a part on the inside of an organism that helps it survive, even though you can't see it from outside. A plant's roots absorb water and nutrients from the soil, functioning even underground. A fish's gills let it pull oxygen from water, the same job your lungs do with air. Compare gills and lungs: how are their jobs similar, even though they work in different environments?
You just compared internal structures across two very different environments! Tomorrow we'll learn about structures for sensing the environment.

objectives: Define an internal structure as a non-visible body part that helps an organism survive
Compare gills and lungs as structures with the same job in different environments
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's external-structures work.
2. Introduce internal structures using the roots/gills examples.
3. Have the child compare gills and lungs.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's sensing-structures lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a simple diagram of a fish and a person to visually compare gills and lungs, rather than describing from memory alone
Ready for more: ask the child to think of another internal structure (like a heart or stomach) and explain its survival function
The gills/lungs comparison is the strongest example here for building the 'same job, different environment' idea that recurs later this week
teacherGuide.answerKey: Gills and lungs both pull oxygen from the organism's environment (water for gills, air for lungs) so the organism can breathe — same job, different environment.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS Grade 4 Life Science standard 4-LS1-1, extending yesterday's external-structure model to internal structures.
